cat.habitat: Homes and a wide range of natural habitats worldwide
facts: Cats have excellent night vision.
Whiskers help cats sense nearby objects and narrow spaces.
Dogs were domesticated from wolves more than 15,000 years ago.
A dog's sense of smell is thousands of times more sensitive than a human's.
Cows have four stomach compartments to digest tough plant material.
They can recognise many individual herd members.
Oxen are adult cattle, usually castrated males, trained to pull loads.
They have been used for ploughing and transport for thousands of years.

buffalo.habitat: Wetlands, river valleys and farmland in Asia and Africa
facts: Water buffalo love to wallow in mud and water to cool off.
They are important farm animals for milk and field work in South Asia.
Horses can sleep both standing up and lying down.
A horse's eyes sit on the sides of its head, giving it a very wide field of view.
Sheep have rectangular pupils that give them a wide view of their surroundings.
They are one of the earliest animals domesticated by humans.
Goats are excellent climbers and can balance on steep rocky ledges.
Their rectangular pupils let them see almost 360 degrees.
Pigs are considered among the most intelligent farm animals.
They do not sweat much, so they wallow in mud to keep cool.

rabbit.habitat: Meadows, woodland edges, burrows and homes
facts: A rabbit's teeth never stop growing.
Rabbits can rotate their ears to pick up sounds from different directions.
Hares are born with fur and open eyes and can run soon after birth.
They can reach speeds of around 60 km/h.
Donkeys are well adapted to dry, harsh environments.
They have a very strong memory for places and other animals.

lion.habitat: African savannas and grasslands (a small population lives in India's Gir Forest)
facts: Lions are the only big cats that live in social groups called prides.
A lion's roar can be heard from about 8 km away.

tiger.habitat: Forests, mangroves and grasslands of Asia
facts: Every tiger has a unique stripe pattern, like a fingerprint.
Tigers are the largest living cat species and are strong swimmers.

leopard.habitat: Forests, savannas, mountains and even areas near cities in Africa and Asia
facts: Leopards often carry their prey up into trees to protect it.
Their rosette-shaped spots help them blend into dappled light.

cheetah.habitat: Open savannas and grasslands, mainly in Africa
facts: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching about 100 km/h in short sprints.
Cheetahs cannot roar; they chirp and purr instead.

elephant.habitat: Savannas, forests and grasslands of Africa and Asia
facts: Elephants are the largest land animals on Earth.
Their trunks contain tens of thousands of muscle units and can pick up a single peanut.
Many bears hibernate or enter a deep winter sleep to survive food shortages.
Bears have an excellent sense of smell, far better than a dog's.

wolf.habitat: Forests, tundra, mountains and grasslands of the Northern Hemisphere
facts: Wolves live and hunt in family groups called packs.
Howling helps wolves communicate across long distances.

fox.habitat: Forests, grasslands, deserts, tundra and urban areas
facts: Foxes can hear small animals digging underground.
The red fox has the widest geographic range of any wild land carnivore.

coyote.habitat: Prairies, deserts, forests and cities in North America
facts: Coyotes are highly adaptable and have expanded into cities.
They communicate using howls, yips and barks.
Male deer grow new antlers every year.
Fawns are born with white spots that help camouflage them.
Both male and female reindeer grow antlers.
Their hooves widen in winter to walk on snow and in summer to cross soft ground.

antelope.habitat: Savannas, grasslands and deserts, mostly in Africa and Asia
facts: Many antelopes can leap and sprint rapidly to escape predators.
Unlike deer, antelopes keep their horns for life.
Monkeys live in social groups and communicate with calls and gestures.
Many New World monkeys have tails that can grip branches.

gorilla.habitat: Tropical and mountain forests of central Africa
facts: Gorillas are the largest living primates.
Adult males are called silverbacks because of the silver hair on their backs.

chimpanzee.habitat: Rainforests and woodland savannas of Africa
facts: Chimpanzees use tools, such as sticks, to get insects.
They share about 98% of their DNA with humans.
The name means 'person of the forest' in Malay.
Orangutans build a new sleeping nest in the trees almost every night.
No two zebras have exactly the same stripe pattern.
A zebra foal can stand and walk within about an hour of birth.

panda.habitat: Bamboo forests in the mountains of central China
facts: A giant panda can eat 12 kg or more of bamboo a day.
Pandas have an enlarged wrist bone that works like a thumb for gripping bamboo.

hippopotamus.habitat: Rivers, lakes and swamps of sub-Saharan Africa
facts: Hippos spend most of the day in water to protect their skin from the sun.
Despite their size, they can run faster than a human over short distances.

hyena.habitat: Savannas, grasslands and semi-deserts of Africa and Asia
facts: Spotted hyenas are skilled hunters, not just scavengers.
They have extremely strong jaws that can crush bone.

rhinoceros.habitat: Grasslands, savannas and forests of Africa and Asia
facts: A rhino's horn is made of keratin, the same material as human hair and nails.
Several rhino species are critically endangered because of poaching.

camel.habitat: Deserts of Africa, the Middle East and Asia
facts: A camel's hump stores fat, not water.
Camels have long eyelashes and closable nostrils to keep out sand.

kangaroo.habitat: Grasslands, forests and scrublands of Australia
facts: Kangaroos cannot walk backwards easily.
Baby kangaroos (joeys) continue to develop inside their mother's pouch.
Koalas sleep up to 18-22 hours a day.
They are not bears; they are marsupials.

wombat.habitat: Forests, mountains and heathland of Australia
facts: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings.
They dig large burrow systems with powerful claws.

possum.habitat: Forests, farmland and suburbs of the Americas and Australasia
facts: Opossums in the Americas are the only marsupials found north of Mexico.
Some opossums 'play dead' when threatened.

okapi.habitat: Rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
facts: The okapi is the closest living relative of the giraffe.
Its striped legs resemble a zebra's, but it is not related to zebras.

bison.habitat: Prairies, grasslands and forests of North America and Europe
facts: Bison are the largest land mammals in North America.
They can run at about 55 km/h despite their size.

boar.habitat: Forests, woodlands and farmland across Eurasia and beyond
facts: Wild boars are the ancestors of domestic pigs.
They use their snouts to dig for roots and insects.
Badgers live in large underground burrow systems called setts.
They are mostly active at night.

bat.habitat: Caves, forests, buildings and cities worldwide
bat.diet: Insectivore, fruit-eater or nectar-feeder depending on species
facts: Bats are the only mammals capable of true, sustained flight.
Many bats use echolocation to find food in the dark.
Hedgehogs curl into a spiny ball when threatened.
A hedgehog has thousands of spines.
Porcupine quills detach easily when touched by a predator.
Some porcupines are skilled tree climbers.

raccoon.habitat: Forests, wetlands and cities in North America
facts: Raccoons have very sensitive front paws and often 'wash' their food.
They are active mostly at night.
Sea otters hold hands while sleeping so they do not drift apart.
Otters have the densest fur of any animal, with up to a million hairs per square inch (sea otters).

seal.habitat: Oceans and coasts, especially cold waters
facts: Seals can hold their breath for many minutes while diving.
A thick layer of blubber keeps them warm in cold water.
Dolphins use echolocation to find food and navigate.
They communicate with whistles and clicks and live in social groups called pods.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived.
Whales are mammals: they breathe air and feed their calves milk.
Squirrels bury thousands of nuts each year and forget some, which grow into trees.
Their bushy tails help with balance and keep them warm.
A mouse's teeth never stop growing.
Mice have an excellent sense of smell and hearing.
Rats are intelligent and can learn mazes quickly.
They are strong swimmers and climbers.
Hamsters store food in their cheek pouches.
Most hamsters are nocturnal.

eagle.habitat: Mountains, forests, coasts and open country
facts: Eagles can spot prey from several kilometres away.
Many eagles build huge nests and reuse them for years.

parrot.habitat: Tropical and subtropical forests and woodlands
facts: Many parrots can imitate human speech.
Parrots have strong curved beaks and zygodactyl feet (two toes forward, two back).

owl.habitat: Forests, grasslands, deserts and farmland worldwide
facts: Owls can rotate their heads about 270 degrees.
Their feathers are soft, letting them fly almost silently.

peacock.habitat: Forests and farmland of South Asia
facts: Only males (peacocks) have the colourful train of feathers.
The Indian peafowl is the national bird of India.
Crows are among the most intelligent birds and can use tools.
They can recognise individual human faces.
Pigeons have been used to carry messages for thousands of years.
They have a remarkable ability to find their way home.
House sparrows live closely with humans.
Sparrows are social and often feed in flocks.

flamingo.habitat: Shallow lakes, lagoons and coastal wetlands
facts: Flamingos get their pink colour from pigments in their food.
They often stand on one leg, which may help them conserve body heat.

penguin.habitat: Coasts and oceans of the Southern Hemisphere, especially Antarctica
facts: Penguins cannot fly, but they are superb swimmers.
Emperor penguin fathers incubate the egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter.
Ducks have waterproof feathers coated with oil from a gland near the tail.
Ducklings can swim within hours of hatching.
Geese often migrate in V-shaped formations.
They form strong, long-lasting pair bonds.
Swans mate for life in many species.
Young swans are called cygnets.
Chickens descend from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia.
A hen can lay a few hundred eggs a year, depending on breed.

turkey.habitat: Woodlands and farms, native to North America
facts: Male turkeys fan their tails and gobble to attract mates.
Wild turkeys can fly short distances and roost in trees.
The ostrich is the largest and heaviest living bird.
It can run at about 70 km/h.

toucan.habitat: Tropical rainforests of Central and South America
facts: The large colourful bill is light because it is mostly hollow.
Toucans use their bills to reach fruit on thin branches.

hummingbird.habitat: Forests, gardens and meadows of the Americas
facts: Hummingbirds can hover and even fly backwards.
Their wings can beat dozens of times per second.

hornbill.habitat: Tropical forests and savannas of Africa and Asia
facts: Hornbills have a large curved bill topped with a casque.
In many species the female is sealed inside a tree hollow while nesting.
Woodpeckers drum on trees to find insects and communicate.
Special skull structure helps absorb the shock of pecking.
Sandpipers probe mud and sand with long bills to find food.
Many species migrate thousands of kilometres each year.
This group of water birds includes pelicans, herons, ibises and spoonbills.
Pelicans have a large throat pouch used to scoop up fish.

snake.habitat: Forests, deserts, grasslands, wetlands and oceans (most regions except Antarctica)
facts: Snakes smell by flicking their forked tongues.
Most snakes are not venomous, but all wild snakes should be left alone.

turtle.diet: Omnivore, herbivore or carnivore depending on species
facts: A turtle's shell is part of its skeleton, fused to its spine and ribs.
Sea turtles return to the beaches where they hatched to lay eggs.

crocodile.habitat: Rivers, lakes, swamps and coasts in tropical regions
facts: Crocodiles have changed little in millions of years.
They have one of the strongest bites of any animal.

lizard.habitat: Deserts, forests, grasslands and homes worldwide
lizard.diet: Insectivore, omnivore or carnivore depending on species
facts: Many lizards can drop their tails to escape predators, and regrow them.
Chameleons can move their eyes independently.
Frogs start life as tadpoles in water.
Many frogs absorb water and oxygen through their skin.
Fish breathe underwater using gills.
There are more than 30,000 known species of fish.
Goldfish were first bred in China over a thousand years ago.
They can recognise their owners and learn simple routines.
A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, not bone.
Sharks can replace lost teeth throughout their lives.

seahorse.habitat: Shallow tropical and temperate coastal waters
facts: Male seahorses carry the eggs and give birth to the young.
They swim upright and hold on to plants with their tails.

butterfly.habitat: Meadows, forests, gardens and wetlands worldwide
facts: Butterflies go through complete metamorphosis: egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult.
They taste with sensors on their feet.

moth.habitat: Forests, fields, gardens and cities worldwide
moth.diet: Nectar or none (some adults do not eat)
facts: Most moths are active at night.
Moths and butterflies belong to the same order, Lepidoptera.

caterpillar.habitat: Plants in forests, fields and gardens
facts: Caterpillars are the larval stage of butterflies and moths.
A caterpillar's main job is to eat and grow before forming a pupa.
Bees pollinate many of the crops people eat.
Honey bees communicate food locations by dancing.

beetle.habitat: Almost every land and freshwater habitat
facts: Beetles are the largest group of animals, with hundreds of thousands of species.
Their front wings form hard cases that protect the flying wings.
A ladybug can eat many aphids a day, helping gardeners.
Their bright colours warn predators that they taste bad.
Dragonflies have existed for about 300 million years.
Each of their four wings can move independently.
Grasshoppers can jump many times their body length.
Many species make sounds by rubbing their legs against their wings.

fly.diet: Varies: nectar, decaying matter or other liquids
facts: Flies have only one pair of wings; the second pair is reduced to tiny balancing organs.
Their compound eyes detect movement very quickly.
Only female mosquitoes bite, using blood for egg development.
Mosquitoes spread diseases such as malaria and dengue.

cockroach.habitat: Homes, forests and sewers in warm regions
facts: Cockroaches have lived on Earth for hundreds of millions of years.
Some species can survive for weeks without food.
Spiders have eight legs and are not insects.
Not all spiders spin webs; some hunt or ambush prey.
Crabs walk sideways.
They shed their hard shell as they grow.
Lobsters have blue blood.
They can regrow lost claws and legs.

octopus.habitat: Oceans, from coral reefs to the deep sea
facts: Octopuses have three hearts.
They can change colour and texture to camouflage themselves.
Squid move by jet propulsion.
Giant squid have the largest eyes of any animal.
Oysters filter large amounts of water each day.
Some oysters produce pearls.
Jellyfish have no brain, heart or bones.
Their bodies are more than 90% water.
Starfish (sea stars) can regenerate lost arms.
They move using hundreds of tiny tube feet.
